newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin conspicuous by absence as CIS gathers.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin conspicuous by absence as CIS gathers.

text.p: Prime ministers from former Soviet republics grouped in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) will meet in Moscow on Friday but the event is overshadowed by Russian President Boris Yeltsin's illness.

It was originally planned as a full heads of state summit chaired by Yeltsin. But the 65-year-old president, who underwent a heart bypass operation in November, will spend a ninth day in hospital with pneumonia.

The meeting of heads of state, marking the fifth anniversary of the founding of the CIS on the ruins of the Soviet Union and already postponed from December, has been put off until the end of the month.
Doctors said on Thursday Yeltsin's condition had "stabilised significantly" and he worked on papers for two hours.
They have forecast he will be well enough to chair a CIS summit by around January 30 but no firm date has been set.

Yeltsin's political opponents have turned up the heat since his latest illness thwarted his ambition to get down to much-needed business after half a year on the sidelines with heart trouble. A leading communist lawmaker shelved a motion to have parliament oust the president -- but only for a few days.

Viktor Ilyukhin said he shelved a bid to put the motion to the house on Friday after legal experts ruled it invalid. But he still plans to put it to a vote on January 22. It is virtually impossible, however, for parliament to unseat the president.

Some analysts argue that Russia has been run reasonably smoothly in the president's absence by his administration and by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's government and suggest that this situation could continue for some time. Chernomyrdin will be back to chair Friday's CIS meeting after a week's holiday.

Others, however, forecast that the longer Yeltsin remains out of sight -- he has not even been shown on television since entering the Central Clinical Hospital on January 8 -- the more politics will be distracted by manoeuvring over an eventual succession and the longer urgent decisions will be put off.

Former security adviser Alexander Lebed continued his one-man presidential campaign. Visiting Germany this week, he plans to be in Washington for Bill Clinton's inauguration on Monday -- despite irritated White House denials after Lebed insisted he had a personal invitation from the U.S. president.

A new poll showed more than one Russian in two trusted the outspoken former general compared to less than one in four who had confidence in Yeltsin. Lebed told ORT television he expected wide backing for his presidential bid. He has said he expects an election this year, although Yeltsin's term ends only in 2000.
Among urgent policy work pressing on the Kremlin is the quest for a deal with NATO on the western defence alliance's plan to admit former Soviet-bloc countries in eastern Europe.
Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov repeated on Thursday that Russia remained firmly opposed to NATO's plans but said Moscow would not respond by creating its own new military bloc.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana is due to meet Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Moscow on Monday. However, Yeltsin will want the last word on any deal with NATO this year.
Valery Serov, a Russian deputy prime minister, said Friday's meeting, attended by 10 of the 12 CIS governments, would concentrate on economic integration.
Moscow's relations with its former empire remain uneven. Yeltsin has suggested a union with Belarus. But relations with Russia's bigger western neighbour, Ukraine, remain rocky.

Five years after the collapse of its Soviet dominion, Moscow is also concerned about further territorial losses. A leading liberal legislator hit out on Thursday at Europe's OSCE for giving Chechnya's rebel leaders money to run an election.
Moscow agreed to the election after a ceasefire last autumn. But Kremlin human rights adviser Vladimir Katashkin said on Thursday the January 27 poll would be "blatantly undemocratic".
